capabilities.untrustedWorkspaces.descrip: TypeScript 7 only runs the content mapper in trusted workspaces. In Restricted Mode, the extension explains that @salesforce/... imports aren't declared until you trust the workspace.

configuration.title: Lightning Bolts
configuration.maintainLwcConfigs.markdow:
Keep the `lwc` folders' `jsconfig.json` and `tsconfig.json` files in the shape the content mapper needs, restoring them at startup and whenever they change. Only the parts the mapper depends on are changed; the rest of each file is kept.

Off, the extension never changes these files, and only says when one needs updating. [Learn more](https://github.com/aheber/lwc-bolts/blob/main/packages/vscode-extension/docs/setup.md#keeping-configs-in-step)
configuration.contentMapper.apexNamespac: Use an identifier or a dotted path of identifiers, such as Apex or Acme.Apex.

For metadata files outside a project config (`jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`): the namespace Apex classes are declared in. Set to `null` to declare them globally, where they can merge with global types of the same name.

Projects with a config use its `apexNamespace` option instead; **Lightning Bolts: Apply Content Mapper Settings to Project Config** copies this setting there.
configuration.contentMapper.inaccessible: Declare them as `@deprecated`, so editors flag code that reads them.
Declare them like the fields LWC can read.
Leave them out, which makes reading one an error.

For metadata files outside a project config (`jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`): how to declare Apex class fields LWC can't read (not `@AuraEnabled`, not `public` or `global`, or `static`). SObject fields are always declared.

Projects with a config use its `inaccessibleApexProperties` option instead; **Lightning Bolts: Apply Content Mapper Settings to Project Config** copies this setting there.
configuration.contentMapper.respectForce:
For metadata files outside a project config (`jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`): skip files the SFDX project's `.forceignore` excludes, as the Salesforce CLI does when deploying: their `@salesforce/...` modules aren't declared, and their templates aren't checked. Off, they're mapped like any other file.

Projects with a config use its `respectForceIgnore` option instead; **Lightning Bolts: Apply Content Mapper Settings to Project Config** copies this setting there.
configuration.contentMapper.suppressDiag: Use a file extension that starts with a dot, such as .cls.

For metadata files outside a project config (`jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`): file extensions, such as `.cls`, whose files don't show TypeScript errors, matched case-insensitively. By default, every extension the mapper handles; set `[]` to show every error.

Projects with a config use its `suppressDiagnosticsExtensions` option instead; **Lightning Bolts: Apply Content Mapper Settings to Project Config** copies this setting there. There, the default suppresses none.
configuration.contentMapper.useVSCodeNod:
For metadata files outside a project config (`jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`): run the content mapper with VS Code's built-in Node.js instead of the `node` on your `PATH`. The `node` on your `PATH` is still used when VS Code's Node.js is too old for the mapper.

Projects with a config always run the `node` on your `PATH`.
configuration.contentMapper.disabledMeta:
For metadata files outside a project config (`jsconfig.json` or `tsconfig.json`): metadata types whose `@salesforce/...` modules aren't declared.

Projects with a config use its `disabledMetadataTypes` option instead; **Lightning Bolts: Apply Content Mapper Settings to Project Config** copies this setting there.
